summary: Scott Wu, co-founder and CEO of Cognition AI, introduces Devin as a fully autonomous software engineer with access to the same tools as human engineers—planning, creating directories, starting apps, reading files, deploying, and making pull requests. The demo shows Devin building a mobile-friendly name game website from a TSV file of approximately 170 World's Fair speakers, iterating via plain English feedback to hide names, restyle buttons, and add a streak counter. Devin is also used in production at Cognition to build Devin itself: team member Bryce tasked Devin with creating a search bar component, Devin followed a repository playbook from a cloned snapshot, made a PR with Phosphor icon feedback, and the PR was merged. Many API integrations, internal dashboards, and metrics tracking were also built by Devin. Wu frames two waves of generative AI: first-wave text-completion products (ChatGPT, Copilot, Cursor) and the emerging agent wave requiring higher consistency. He explains why code pairs well with agents: software engineering involves more than typing code, and code feedback iteration provides a clean problem-solving path. Wu then discusses the novel UX problem of agent design—agents differ from both traditional software and human-human interaction, requiring features like session forking and rollback, Slack/GitHub integrations, playbooks, machine snapshots, secrets management, and a new VS Code Live Share feature for collaborating on Devin's machine. Cognition's workflow has shifted to async parallel tasking: engineers give multiple tasks to multiple Devins simultaneously, described as working with enthusiastic interns. Wu envisions software engineering splitting into two jobs—problem-solving/architecture and implementation—with Devin freeing engineers to focus on the former. He predicts more software engineers than ever, citing precedent from punch cards to assembly to C, with demand for software exceeding 10x current supply and each engineer becoming 5-10x more effective. In Q&A, Wu addresses access ramping, Devin's self-contained dev environment for debugging, junior engineer training evolving around fundamentals, and challenges spanning speed, consistency, integrations, and product UX, aided by a rising tide of hardware, foundation models, and agentic research.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Scott Wu introduces himself from Cognition AI and announces he will discuss the early makings of Devin and the broader space, starting with a custom demo prepared for the World's Fair.

sections.title: Name Game Demo
sections.summary: Scott demos Devin building a mobile-friendly name game website from a TSV file of approximately 170 World's Fair speakers. Devin autonomously plans, creates a React app, reads the TSV, and deploys a first version. Scott then gives plain English feedback to hide names until clicked, restyle the play again button, and add a streak counter. The final deployed website works as intended.

sections.title: Devin Building Devin
sections.summary: Scott highlights that Devin is used internally to build Devin itself. Team member Bryce tasked Devin with creating a search bar in the sessions list; Devin started from a cloned snapshot with a repository playbook, made a PR, incorporated feedback about a magnifying glass icon using Phosphor icons, and the PR was merged. Many API integrations, dashboards, and metrics tracking were also built by Devin.

sections.title: Company Journey
sections.summary: Cognition started about seven months ago in November, beginning in hacker houses in the Bay Area, then New York, then back to the Bay, growing the team and getting slightly larger Airbnbs each time before now settling in the Bay Area.

sections.title: Why Agents and Why Code
sections.summary: Wu frames two waves of generative AI: first-wave text-completion products (ChatGPT, Copilot, Cursor) and the emerging agent wave with autonomous decision-making. He explains why code pairs well with agents: software engineering involves more than typing code, the ability to iterate with code feedback provides a clean problem-solving path, and model agentic capabilities are improving rapidly. He notes both a deep capabilities challenge and a novel UX design problem in agent development.

sections.title: Agent UX and Product Features
sections.summary: Wu explains that agent UX is fundamentally different from both traditional software and human-human interaction, involving nuances of parallel work, information gathering, and context management. He lists product features built into Devin: shell access, code editing, web browsing, session forking and rollback, Slack and GitHub integrations, playbooks, machine snapshots, secrets management, and verification tools. He showcases a newly shipped feature: VS Code Live Share on Devin's machine, enabling collaborative editing where engineers can make edits and talk with Devin.

sections.title: Parallel Devin Workflow and Async Collaboration
sections.summary: Wu describes how Cognition's workflow has shifted to async parallel tasking: engineers assign multiple tasks to multiple Devins running simultaneously, turning every engineer into an engineering manager. He compares Devins to enthusiastic interns who try hard but get little things wrong and ask questions. He shares a fun example from that day of asking Devin via Slack to change a color, Devin making the PR, and merging it. He notes the ability to describe tasks to Devin from a phone and review code afterward.

sections.title: Future of Software Engineering
sections.summary: Wu frames software engineering as two jobs: problem-solving with code (architecture, flows, edge cases) and implementation (debugging, unit tests, etc.). He estimates engineers spend ~10-20% on the former and ~80-90% on the latter, and sees Devin freeing engineers to focus on problem-solving, becoming a mix of technical architect and product manager. He predicts more software engineers than ever, citing precedent from punch cards to assembly to C, with demand for software exceeding 10x current supply and each engineer becoming 5-10x more effective.

sections.title: Q&A
sections.summary: Wu addresses audience questions: access is ramping up weekly with enterprise customers but a large waitlist remains; Devin has a fully instantiated dev environment in the codebase for reproducing and debugging issues; junior engineers will still need fundamentals (understanding problems, architectures, edge cases) though training will evolve; and the biggest challenges to realizing the vision span speed, consistency, access, integrations, and product UX, with a rising tide of hardware, foundation models, and agentic research driving improvements across the stack.
